metadata.title: PISA 2006: Science Competencies for Tomorrow’s World, Vol. 1

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis is based on the OECD PISA 2006 international survey design, where students are sampled within schools and schools within participating countries. The report describes that around 400,000 students were randomly selected to represent about 20 million 15-year-olds across 57 participating countries, and that test booklets were randomly assigned to students. For school-principal questionnaire responses, the report states that responses are weighted so they are proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in the school. The excerpt does not specify the exact student weight variable name(s) or any replicate-weight scheme; therefore, the weighting approach is described at the design level rather than by variable code.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This extraction is for an OECD PISA 2006 volume that reports descriptive and multilevel associations using PISA science scores and proficiency distributions, rather than an empirical ML model with an explicitly documented PV-combining or missing-data-imputation procedure in the provided text. Plausible values handling is therefore not applicable for this extraction because the excerpt does not document PV estimation/combining steps for an ML pipeline. Missing-data handling is not reported in the provided excerpt because the text focuses on substantive results and policy implications, while detailed technical procedures are deferred to the PISA 2006 Technical Report and annexes not included here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The excerpt describes the PISA 2006 target population as 15-year-olds aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months who have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, regardless of school type (public/private, academic/vocational). It also notes that exclusions are limited (overall exclusion rate kept below 5% and typically below 6% in all countries, with specific limits for school-level and within-school exclusions). No additional analytic subsample restrictions (e.g., specific assessment modules or grade-only filters) are specified in the provided text for the school/system association results; therefore, the analysis is treated as using the full available PISA 2006 sample for the countries included in the reported figures/tables.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2006 volume reports student performance in science (and also updates for reading and mathematics) using the PISA assessment framework and proficiency scales. PISA 2006 is administered to 15-year-olds across 57 participating countries/economies, with around 400,000 students sampled to represent about 20 million 15-year-olds. Students complete pencil-and-paper tasks (with a computer-delivered science component in a subset of countries) and a student questionnaire, while school principals complete a school questionnaire. Science performance is reported on a continuous science scale (mean OECD=500) and grouped into six proficiency levels, with additional reporting by science competencies and knowledge domains. The excerpt further describes multilevel modeling of between-school variance and net associations between school/system characteristics and science performance, including how much between-school variation is explained and which school factors remain statistically significant after accounting for demographic and socio-economic context. The report emphasizes that these are associations and that policy interpretation must consider methodological caveats and the limits of large-scale survey data.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is extracted from an OECD PISA 2006 technical/policy volume rather than an empirical ML paper. The provided excerpt does not specify an ML prediction pipeline, target variables for ML, or algorithmic model comparisons; instead it reports PISA scoring, proficiency benchmarks, and multilevel associations. As a result, fields required for empirical ML extraction (e.g., main_findings rows, ML techniques, and conceptual confounder lists for predictors in an ML model) are intentionally left empty.
